item.title: Section 144 imposed in Habiganj amid BNP-NCP tensions
item.description:
Habiganj District Administrator Dr GM Sarfaraz has imposed Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1898, in the municipal area amid tensions between the BNP and National Citizen Party (NCP).
He imposed the restrictions through a notice issued at 10am on Wednesday.
According to the notice, the NCP had called a rally in the Habiganj municipal area on Wednesday. At the same time and at the same venue, Habiganj municipal BNP and the district unit of Chhatra Dal had also called a protest rally.
The district magistrate said tensions had emerged between the two sides over the programmes, raising concerns that the law and order situation could deteriorate.
As a result, under Section 144, all types of meetings, rallies and the use of loudspeakers have been banned in the municipal area.
The district administration has instructed the police to enforce the order in the public interest.

item.title: Hawkers need solutions beyond evictions
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directive to swiftly rehabilitate hawkers evicted from Dhaka’s streets is a necessary intervention in a problem that has dragged on for far too long.
Hawkers are not criminals but workers, and a key part of our informal economy. When they are evicted without a plan, the consequences are immediate and severe.
Creating a situation where they struggle to earn, or are forced to operate in unsafe or unsuitable locations, or pushed into debt, is not a solution.
The PM’s words must therefore be treated as a directive to rethink how Dhaka handles its informal workforce. Hawkers need designated, well‑planned vending zones, not ad‑hoc spaces that shift with every police operation.
They need clear rules, not arbitrary enforcement along with basic facilities so that their workplaces are dignified and safe. Most importantly, they need formal recognition so that their rights and responsibilities are defined rather than negotiated on the street.
Cities around the world have shown that hawkers can coexist with traffic flow, pedestrian movement, and urban order, but only when the state plans for it. Dhaka’s current approach, built on periodic eviction drives that lead nowhere, has failed repeatedly. All such an approach has achieved is disrupted livelihoods, fueled tension, and ultimately, hawkers returning to the same spots out of necessity.
Hawkers deserve stability, not uncertainty, with a system that acknowledges their role in the economy rather than treating them as obstacles to be removed.
A proper solution therefore requires coordination to ensure that rehabilitation is practical, not symbolic. The PM has set the expectation. Now the administration must deliver.

item.title: SC clears way for Sarwar Alamgir to perform MP duties
item.description:
The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court has removed from its cause list an appeal seeking to bar BNP candidate Sarwar Alamgir from performing his duties as an MP from the Chittagong-2 constituency in the 13th parliamentary election.
As a result, there is no legal bar to his performing his duties as an MP, lawyers said. However, Jamaat-e-Islami candidate for the constituency may file a regular appeal against the High Court verdict if he wishes.
A four-member Appellate Division bench headed by the Chief Justice Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury passed the order on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, an appeal seeking to prevent BNP candidate Sarwar Alamgir from attending parliamentary sessions after taking his oath as an MP was scheduled for an order on Tuesday, but no order was issued. The matter was heard again that day, after which the Appellate Division set a new date for delivering its order.
Earlier, the High Court declared the Election Commission’s decision upholding Sarwar Alamgir’s candidacy illegal. Jamaat candidate for Chittagong-2, Muhammad Nurul Amin, filed an appeal against the verdict.
Nurul Amin sought a stay on the operation of the High Court verdict and an injunction preventing Sarwar Alamgir from attending parliamentary sessions until the appeal is disposed of.
Lawyers Ahsanul Karim and AM Mahbub Uddin Khokon appeared for Sarwar Alamgir, while Mohammad Shishir Monir and Azim Uddin Patwari represented Muhammad Nurul Amin.
Earlier, an application was filed with the Appellate Division seeking an order preventing Sarwar Alamgir from attending Parliament. In the application, Nurul Amin sought a ban on Sarwar Alamgir’s participation in parliamentary proceedings until the appeal is resolved.
After the returning officer declared Sarwar Alamgir’s candidacy valid, rival candidate Nurul Amin appealed to the Election Commission, alleging that Sarwar was a loan defaulter. Following a hearing, the Election Commission cancelled Sarwar Alamgir’s nomination on January 18.
Challenging the decision, Sarwar Alamgir filed a writ petition with the High Court. On January 27, the High Court stayed the Election Commission’s order and issued a rule allowing him to contest the election. Nurul Amin subsequently sought leave to appeal before the Appellate Division, which granted leave on February 3.
At the same time, although Sarwar Alamgir was allowed to contest the election, the court ordered that the publication of the election results be withheld until the appeal was disposed of.

item.title: Barrister Mosharraf Hossain takes charge as CID chief
item.description:
Additional Inspector General of Police (Addl IGP) Barrister Mohammad Mosharraf Hossain on Wednesday formally assumed charge as the chief of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID).
Earlier, he served as Director of the National Security Intelligence (NSI), according to a gazette notification issued on Tuesday.
A 15th BCS Police cadre officer, he joined Bangladesh Police as an ASP in 1995.
During his nearly three decade career, he served in CID, DMP, CMP, RAB, Police Headquarters, Police Academy Sardah and as superintendent of police in Pirojpur and Chapainawabganj, gaining extensive experience in investigation, intelligence, training and administration.
He holds a master's degree in Economics from Islamic University, Kushtia, and a Bar-at-Law from City University of London, UK, and has received specialised training in forensic science and modern policing at home and abroad.
Senior CID officials welcomed him at the charge-taking ceremony.

item.title: What freedom is and is not
item.description:
In an era of rising authoritarianism, democratic backsliding, and governments across the world wrapping repression in the language of liberty, On Freedom (Crown, 2024) by historian Timothy Snyder is a passionate plea to uphold freedom as the foundation of all political activity. To him, freedom is not a value to be chanted but rather a series of activities that ensure the realization of potential inherent to every human being. His focus in this book is distinguishing negative freedom, or freedom from, from positive freedom, or freedom to.
Negative freedom is a conception of freedom that defines freedom as the removal of certain obstacles only—which can be race, ethnicity, class, or a colonizer. Snyder gives the example of the colonized states, which failed to recognize that breaking free from the colonizers was only the beginning of their struggle. Positive freedom, on the other hand, is recognizing that freedom is always freedom to do activities that are essential to ensure that freedom is for everyone. Positive freedom is the route to make freedom available for everyone, not a select few with state or corporate power. Snyder puts forward five forms of this freedom—sovereignty, unpredictability, mobility, factuality, and solidarity.
The first chapter is on sovereignty. Snyder introduces two terms, which he recounts throughout the book—Leib and Körper. The former means a living body, where "living" includes the ability to govern itself, whereas "Körper" means just a body, subject to physical laws. Snyder brings up the Covid-19 vaccine crisis, where big pharmaceuticals treated the bodies of the victims as Körper to profit, not Leib to save. This fundamental empathy of treating oneself as a sovereign Leib and treating others as such is being free.
Unpredictability, the second form, is perhaps the most counterintuitive. Being unpredictable means being creative, recognizing the differences within humans while being cooperative. He encourages his readers to be unpredictable, to not be led by political demagogues and social media, but rather to appreciate creativity and the realization of new values through multiple combinations of them.
The third form is mobility. This part focuses on the state’s role in creating opportunities for its citizens. Mobility was the crux of the American Dream, and it was largely a result of Roosevelt’s New Deal and other social and economic programs to facilitate it. But in the Reagan era, these rights were overturned, with Reagan arguing that “the state” was the obstacle to freedom. In practice, these meant freedom only for oligarchs. To build freedom for everyone, social mobility is essential. Without social mobility, one cannot be sovereign or unpredictable—they have to be suppressed either under the state or the so-called free market, and that is unfreedom.
Factuality, the fourth form, takes on particular urgency in an era of conspiracy theories, AI-generated misinformation, and climate change denialism. Snyder's argument is that historically, freedom of speech was about speaking truth to power and protecting the people who spoke truth to power, and it should be exercised with responsibility to be scientific and fact-based.
Lastly, he discusses solidarity as a form of freedom, because no one is actually free while others are unfree. Without solidarity, divisions are inevitable, and they collectively reduce everyone’s freedom. Therefore, Snyder remarks, an individual cannot be free on his own—they needs structures that have been built by previous generations and the support of others who take care of them.
The book closes with a warning directed at democracies that perform the aesthetics of freedom while institutionalizing its opposite. For Bangladesh and Syria, countries that have recently removed authoritarian governments, this is not an abstract concern. Snyder's message is pointed: removing a dictator is negative freedom. What comes after, the slow, collective, continuous work of building institutions that make freedom real for everyone, is where the harder struggle begins.
On Freedom is not without its gaps. Snyder's focus on the American and European experience means the Global South appears mostly as illustration rather than subject. Readers in Dhaka will find the framework useful but will need to do their own work applying it to a political context Snyder does not fully reckon with. That is a limitation worth naming. But the book's core argument—that freedom is a practice, not a possession, and that it requires structures, solidarity, and honesty to survive—is one that travels.
Sadman Ahmed Siam is a student at the Islamic University of Technology.

item.title: Supporting medical innovation
item.description:
We are encouraged by the support for locally developed medical devices -- and one that Bangladesh’s health sector has needed for a long time.
For decades, the country has relied heavily on imported medical equipment, from diagnostic tools to surgical instruments to hospital monitoring systems. That dependence has made our already fragile healthcare facilities costlier, slowed down access, and left hospitals vulnerable.
While we will not fix our healthcare facilities overnight, and there remain a myriad of issues, this particular story highlights a crucial shift: Bangladesh is beginning to recognize that medical innovation at home is essential.
What is needed now is ensuring sufficient investment for local researchers and manufacturers, so that there are devices that are affordable, context‑appropriate, and tailored to the needs of Bangladeshi patients.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s public endorsement for these efforts sends a message to regulators, investors, and the health industry that domestic innovation in this sector deserves serious attention. Bangladesh must now invest strategically to slowly but surely reduce its reliance on imports.
The economic case is clear. Bangladesh spends significant foreign currency on imported medical equipment every year. Developing a domestic manufacturing ecosystem would not only reduce that burden but also create skilled jobs, expand export potential, and improve resilience during crises.
The public health case is even stronger. Locally produced devices can be designed for Bangladesh’s realities: Rural clinics with limited electricity, hospitals with high patient loads, and communities that need affordable diagnostics. Innovation rooted in local needs is more effective than imported solutions designed for entirely different contexts.
The PM’s endorsement is a positive step. Now the country must build on it with policy, investment, and long‑term commitment. Bangladesh has the talent, the demand, and the urgency. What it needs is a coordinated push to turn local medical innovation into a national strength.

item.title: The meme thief
item.description:
The boy’s name is Rafiq, though hardly anyone remembers it anymore. Online he goes by Bhoot Jolokia, a name borrowed from the world’s hottest chili. His followers call him Bhoot for short, half in awe, half in fear. By day, he is just another Dhaka University student struggling to stretch his money across rising food prices, hostel rent, and never-ending load-shedding. By night, though, his phone becomes a factory of laughter and fire.
Rafiq’s tiny room in a peeling dormitory smells of damp clothes and stale Singara wrappers. A fan rattles above him like an old tin can in the wind. Outside, the traffic roars endlessly down Nilkhet Road. But on his cracked phone screen, the world bends to his humor. He lifts screenshots of political speeches, photos of overpaid cricketers, and stills of ministers cutting ribbons at useless “inaugurations.” With a flick of his thumbs, captions bloom like thorns:
“Dhaka Metro Rail: Motijheel to Kamalapur, 1000 crores gone. Slow and steady robs the race.”
“Minister says onions are cheaper this year. My tears disagree.”
Within minutes, thousands of people share his posts. People from all walks of life scroll through their Android phones during lunch breaks and laugh at them. Even private university students in Bashundhara whisper the memes like they’re contraband jokes. His humor does what no slogan or rally can: it slips past fear.
But Rafiq knows the danger. Satire in Bangladesh walks a knife’s edge. In his childhood, he had heard stories of editors jailed for cartoons and writers harassed for tweets. He remembers the silence after the Holey Artisan attack, when everyone feared words could turn fatal.
Still, he continues. He tells himself he is not a revolutionary. He is a trickster—slippery and ambiguous. If the king dislikes the joke, he can always say, “It was just chili, bhai. Don’t take it so seriously.”
One evening in September, a storm batters Dhaka. Rainwater gushes over the sidewalks, carrying plastic cups and dead rats toward the Buriganga. The power dies, plunging Rafiq’s room into a cave-like dark. He lights a single candle and stares at the latest headline: Parliament approves “Digital Security Act 2.0.”
He laughs bitterly. “Security for whom?” he mutters. Then he crafts a meme:
A minister smiling broadly, the caption—
“New Digital Act: Because laughter is the real national threat.”
He posts it without thinking. The screen glowed briefly before the signal disappeared into the storm.
The next morning, his phone explodes with shares, comments, warnings. "Bro, be careful,” one follower messages. Another writes, “They’ll knock at your door.”
By noon, the meme is on the lips of tea-stall owners at Shahbagh and students marching in New Market. Rafiq watches with a mixture of pride and dread. The trickster has slipped too close to the tiger’s tail.
Two days later, the knock comes.
It is not a violent pounding but a polite tok-tok at the dormitory door. Rafiq opens to find two men in plain clothes, faces expressionless. “We need to talk,” one says. His voice is calm, almost friendly.
They take him to a tea stall instead of a station. One stirs his tea absentmindedly and says, “You are talented. Why waste your time on these dangerous jokes? We can arrange a proper job for you. Design social media campaigns. Earn respect.”
The other adds more sternly, “Stop playing with fire, brother. Jokes can turn into mobs. And mobs—into crimes.”
Rafiq listens, nodding. He said he would think about it. They leave him with a phone number scrawled on tissue paper.
That night, he cannot sleep. He stared at the candle again, thinking of Gopal Bhar—the court jester who survived by laughing with kings, not against them. Was he foolish to resist? Should he accept the offer and sell his wit for comfort?
But then he remembers a message from a clerk at a bank he once met online: “Bhai, your memes make my 10-hour day lighter. Don’t stop.”
The trickster inside him grins. If the king is laughing, the trickster has failed.
So Rafiq begins a new game. He hides his satire inside layers of absurdity.
He posts a photo of a giant Hilsa fish and writes: “Breaking News: Hilsa appointed minister of finance. Experts say it’s the most transparent minister yet.”
He shares an edited video where a politician’s speech is interrupted by a cow mooing.
He invents a character called Baba Onionswami, a mystical guru who predicts inflation by staring at vegetable baskets.
The officials could not decide if these posts were mockery or nonsense. The people, though, understood. The laughter grows sharper, louder, impossible to contain.
One afternoon, while sipping tea at DU Canteen, Rafiq overhears a group of law students analyzing one of his memes as if it were a text in class.
“This one,” a bespectacled boy says, “uses parody to dismantle the state narrative.”
Another adds, “It’s like Bakhtin’s carnival—the inversion of authority through humor.”
Rafiq nearly choked on his tea. He never intended to theory. His memes were like chili—burning quick and crude. But maybe chili, too, could be philosophy.
Then comes December, Victory Day. Dhaka is drenched in green and red. Rafiq creates his boldest meme yet: a photoshopped image of the National Parliament building floating like a boat in floodwater, with the caption—
“Fifty years of independence: Still trying to stay afloat.”
It spreads like wildfire. Some call it art; others call it treason. By evening, TV talk shows debated its meaning.
And then—just as suddenly—it vanishes. Facebook deleted it. His account was locked. Bhoot Jolokia was erased.
For a week, silence. Rafiq walks Dhaka’s streets feeling invisible. He is just another student again, lost in the crowd.
But then, one morning at Nilkhet, he notices a poster on a wall. It shows the Parliament-boat meme, hand-drawn in marker, and the chili logo scrawled at the corner. Beside it, someone has written, "Bhoot lives.”
He walks further. More walls, more posters. Rickshaw hoods painted with chili signs. University bathroom doors scribbled with his jokes. His memes have escaped the phone, growing wilder in the city’s veins.
The trickster could not be caught, he realized. The trickster is never just one person.
Haroonuzzaman is a Bangladeshi translator, novelist, poet, researcher, and academic.

item.title: The shovel and the sword
item.description:
A vanished shrine in a mango orchard. A name scratched off a signboard . A silence where a song used to be . In post-August 5 Bangladesh, what tools do we possess to understand what is being unmade? The answer may lie not in a single book, but in the unexpected conversation between two: a historian’s thesis and a novelist’s hymn.
The delta's counter-narrative
There is a comforting story we tell about Islam in Bengal. It involves armies, edicts, the abrupt replacement of one world by another. It is a story that flatters power. And it is mostly wrong.
Richard M Eaton’s The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier dismantles this fable with the patience of a historian who has learned to listen to the land itself. His argument, distilled, is this: Islam did not conquer Bengal by the sword. It grew here by the shovel. It arrived not primarily through the triumphant procession of armies but through the quiet, centuries-long advance of peasant farmers clearing forests, planting rice, and settling the delta’s shifting, waterlogged frontier.
Behind them came not orthodox theologians but Sufi pirs -- charismatic mystics who spoke the language of the soil, who blessed crops, who translated the austere monotheism of the Quran into metaphors a rice farmer could touch. Eaton calls this a process of “accretion,” not conversion. Islam silted into the delta like the rivers themselves deposited new land: Gradually, imperceptibly, until one day you looked out and realized the landscape had changed.
This is not, in Eaton’s telling, a story of syncretism as weakness or dilution. It is a story of Islam as a living, adaptive force -- one that grew precisely because it could absorb the goddess cults, the harvest rituals, the Bonbibi invocations of the Sundarbans mangrove forest without feeling threatened by them.
The pir’s shrine often stood where a local deity had been worshipped. The fateha was offered with the same hands that had once scattered puja flowers. This was not confusion. It was a civilization making itself.
Why does this matter now ? Because the version of Islam currently ascendant in parts of Bangladesh -- text-obsessed, puritanical, allergic to metaphor -- treats Eaton’s history as heresy. The burning of shrines , the renaming of cultural landmarks, the mob that cannot tolerate a Baul’s ambiguous god : These are not random spasms of violence. They are a systematic assault on a particular way of being Muslim.
And to resist that assault, we need more than outrage. We need memory. We need to recover the texture of the world that is being lost. This is where Syed Mustafa Siraj’s masterpiece Alik Manush enters, stage left, humming a bhatiyali tune.
The novel as living archive
If Eaton gives us the architecture of Bengal’s syncretic Islam -- the land grants, the tax records, the Mughal chronicles -- Siraj gives us its breath. His novel is populated not by historical forces but by people who slosh through the mud of this frontier, whose faith is as soggy and fertile as the soil they till.
Consider the protagonist, a wandering bard whose songs stitch Quranic verses to harvest hymns as naturally as a tailor joins cloth. He does not “perform” syncretism; he inhabits it, the way a fish inhabits water -- unselfconsciously, completely. When he sings, the distinctions that later generations would kill each other over simply dissolve. Is this Islam? Is this Hinduism? The question barely makes sense. It is devotion. It is the delta.
Or take Chhutki, the midwife who delivers babies and prophecies with equal skill. Her spirituality is tactile, rooted in the body -- a counterpoint to the asceticism of the male fakirs who drift through the novel. She knows the incantations for safe childbirth, which happen to invoke both Allah and the forest goddess Bonbibi. She sees no contradiction. The frontier does not demand theological consistency; it demands survival. And survival, in Siraj’s world, requires a certain promiscuity of belief.
There is a moment in the novel -- small, almost throwaway -- where a Hindu widow offers fateha at a pir’s shrine. She does not convert. She does not abandon her gods. She simply adds this gesture to her repertoire of the sacred, the way one might add a new spice to a familiar recipe. Siraj does not explain this. He does not defend it. He simply records it, with the precision of a witness who understands that such moments are the true measure of a civilization.
This is the archive the novel builds: Not a record of doctrines but a choreography of daily life. How people prayed, how they sang, how they bargained with the invisible.
Eaton’s history cannot give us this. The archive of the state -- tax records, land grants, court chronicles -- preserves the decisions of the powerful. It does not preserve the tune a farmer hummed while transplanting rice. It does not record the prayer a midwife whispered. The novel is not a supplement to the history. It is a rival archive, one that stores what power discards as unimportant.
What the text cannot hold
There is a crucial detail in Eaton’s work: Bengal’s conversion to Islam, he notes, was largely an oral process. The Quran was not read; it was sung. Scripture arrived not through the book but through the voice -- through pirs who composed verses in Bangla, through ballads that narrated Islamic sacred history in local poetic forms. The text was secondary. The song was primary.
Siraj’s novel is a tribute to this orality. His characters do not read the Quran; they absorb it through folk songs, through the couplets of wandering minstrels, through the stories told by grandmothers.
Compare this to the Islam of the madrasa, of the text-memorizer, of the cleric who arrives to declare the shrine shirk and the Baul a heretic. The contrast is not just theological. It is civilizational.
One tradition trusts the book; the other trusts the voice. One demands uniformity; the other thrives on variation. The current violence in Bangladesh is, at bottom, an attempt to replace the voice with the book -- to silence the song and install the text as the sole arbiter of the sacred.
This is why Alik Manush feels so urgent now. It is not merely a novel. It is a record of the voice. To read it alongside Eaton is to understand not just how Bengal became Muslim but what kind of Muslim Bengal became -- and what is now at stake.
I have written elsewhere about the mnemonicide underway in Bangladesh. The chainsaws that felled the banyan tree. The machetes that enforce a new orthodoxy. The strange fruit of mob violence, hanging from the branches of a republic in retreat. I will not repeat those arguments here. But I will say this: the destruction is not only physical. It is archival. It is the systematic erasure of a particular past -- the past Eaton documents and Siraj dramatizes.
When a mob burns a pir’s shrine, it is not simply destroying a building. It is declaring that the Islam of the shovel -- the Islam that grew organically, that absorbed and adapted, that produced the music of Lalon and the metaphors of Siraj -- is not Islam at all. It is expelling the delta’s own religious history from the boundaries of the faith. And it is doing so with the confidence of those who believe they alone possess the truth.
So here is what I propose: Read these two books together. Read Eaton to understand the historical soil in which Bengal’s Islam grew. Read Siraj to taste the fruit that soil produced. Read them not as exercises in nostalgia but as acts of retrieval -- because the world they describe is being actively unmade, and because remembering it is a way of refusing to consent to its erasure.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal. His email address is zakir.kibria@gmail.com .

item.title: Beyond duty-free trade
item.description:
As Bangladesh too prepares to graduate from the LDC category, it does not have to wonder what comes next. Since 1994, eight countries have completed the transition. Their experiences show what worked and what did not, and what Bangladesh can expect. Bhutan, one of Bangladesh’s neighbouring counties, lost their duty-free trade benefits soon after graduating. Their experience is an open letter and a roadmap for Bangladesh as it prepares for its own ascent.
The first lesson is a humbling one: None of these countries resembled Bangladesh. A WTO study found around 70% of Bangladesh’s exports receive special trade benefits because it is an LDC. Bhutan’s transition in 2023 was relatively smooth because less than 10% of its exports depended on LDC trade preferences.
Bhutan’s economy primarily relies on hydropower exports to India under commercial agreements rather than LDC preference. The lesson is clear: The best protection is not being dependent on LDC trade benefits. Unfortunately, Bangladesh has yet to build that sort of resilience.
The Maldives points to another important lesson. When it graduated from the LDC list in 2011, its tourism industry was booming. But its fishing industry lost its duty-free access to the European market resulting in high tariffs, making it harder for them to compete.
This illustrates the cost of preparing too late. Cabo Verde, on the other hand, took a calculated approach. Prior to graduating in 2007, it negotiated with the EU for an extension to keep its duty-free access and leveraged that time to fulfill the requirements to join the EU’s GSP+ trade scheme.
As a result, Cabo Verde continued to receive preferential market access even after graduation and remains in the scheme today. Same starting point, different outcomes. Not due to difference in size or wealth -- but rather due to strategic preparation.
The third lesson comes from Samoa, whose strategy began five years before its 2014 graduation, by quietly persuading individual partners like Japan and the United States, to keep granting duty-free access even after its LDC graduation.
Bangladesh appears to be using a similar strategy through its newly formed trade agreement with Japan: Before time runs out, the country will have to secure its market access one country at a time.
Perhaps the most important lesson comes from a country which has not yet graduated. In 2020, the EU suspended Cambodia’s duty-free access on its exports over human rights concerns. About one-fifth of its exports -- including garments, footwear, and travel goods worth about $1 billion -- lost its duty-free access within six months.
The impact was severe. Factories closed and workers lost their jobs. But Cambodia bounced back better than expected. Cambodia responded by redirecting exports to the United States and signing free-trade agreements with China and South Korea. By 2026, the State of Fashion report by McKinsey and The Business of Fashion identified Cambodia as an emerging sourcing hub.
Bangladesh has two lessons to learn from this:
First , trade benefits come with conditions. As demonstrated by Cambodia, the EU’s EBA (Everything But Arms) scheme requires countries to meet certain human rights standards, and failing to meet those standards can result in revoking those benefits.
Second , garment industries can survive losing market access, but only if it is prepared in advance. Cambodia used the time after its setback to diversify its export markets and is due to graduate in 2029.
Our country is at an advantage that Cambodia did not have: To prepare before a crisis hits.
It is of utmost importance that Bangladesh begins preparing now, for the market it will graduate into is very different from the one it grew up serving. The global apparel trend has shifted with shoppers now relying more on thrifted fashion, spending less on new apparel.
Although the market is currently worth nearly $ 2 trillion, that growth is slowing. Fashion brands are rethinking how they source their products. According to this year’s State of Fashion survey, tariffs are now the US’s biggest concern.
To tackle this, they have decided to distribute the risk by spreading production across multiple countries instead of relying on a single supplier. Companies like Zara, for instance, are moving their production closer to Europe, their main market.
Trade rules are becoming more stringent. Due-diligence and traceability laws require exporters to provide proof of meeting standards on labor wages, green production and product origin. Demonstrating compliance is becoming as important as offering competitive prices.
But Bangladesh’s real strength lies elsewhere: A large and experienced garment industry, nearly 300 internationally certified green factories, and a skilled workforce that few competitors can match.
The challenge now is to address its remaining weaknesses with faster production, greater use of man-made fibres, and strengthening the industry of handwoven fabric manufacturing.
Whether we look at the experiences of previous LDC graduates or the changing global apparel industry, the conclusion is the same: The real test is not LDC graduation but staying competitive without the advantage of special treatment like duty-free trade.
Countries like Cabo Verde, which prepared early, transitioned smoothly. Those that delayed, like the Maldives, paid the price. Cambodia faced a greater challenge, yet prevailed.
Bangladesh has been given the syllabus, the case studies, and the tentative timeline. It has the advantage that the others did not. There is still time to prepare, and few excuses if the opportunity is missed.
Abir Mymuny is a former senior manager, Sustainable Finance, City Bank PLC and Consultant in Climate Finance, Circular Capital Analytics LLC, USA.

item.title: 5 Bangladeshi women return home after serving jail terms in India
item.description:
Five Bangladeshi women returned home through Benapole land port on Tuesday night after serving jail terms in India.
Petrapole immigration police handed them over to Benapole immigration police around 8pm under special travel permits.
The returnees were Papia Akter, Shimu Akter, Sharmin Khatun, Lovely Khatun and Rozina Khatun. They are from Jessore, Narail, Bagerhat and Tangail districts.
Officer-in-Charge of Benapole Immigration Police Saifur Rahman said the women entered India through border routes about four years ago after being lured by brokers with promises of jobs.
They were later arrested while working as domestic help and sentenced to two to three years in prison on charges of illegal entry.
After completing their sentences, an Indian human rights organisation kept them at a shelter home. With the cooperation of the high commissions of the two countries and a special travel permit issued by the Indian government, they were repatriated.
Human rights organisation Justice and Care received them and will hand them over to their families.
Justice and Care field facilitator in Jashore Shafiqul Islam said they were taken to a shelter home Tuesday night and would be handed over to their families on Wednesday.

Former minister Latif Siddique arrested
item.description:
Former minister Abdul Latif Siddique has been arrested in a crimes against humanity case filed over the killings during Hefazat-e-Islam's rally at Shapla Chattar in Dhaka's Motijheel.

The Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Detective Branch (DB) arrested him from his residence in Gulshan at around 6:00 pm today, Wednesday, DB Additional Commissioner Md Shafiqul Islam confirmed.

“Latif Siddique has been arrested in a case filed with the International Crimes Tribunal. There was an arrest warrant against him and he was detained accordingly,” Shafiqul Islam told Prothom Alo.

Earlier in the day, Latif Siddique had expressed his intention to surrender before the court in the case. After appearing before Dhaka’s Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Jewel Rana’s court, he said he had decided to surrender.

He added that if he was not arrested beforehand, he would appear before the International Crimes Tribunal on Sunday or Monday next week and seek bail.

Latif Siddique, who was expelled from the Awami League (whose activities now banned), was previously arrested in August last year from an event at the Dhaka Reporters' Unity following the July uprising.

Later, police named him as an accused in a case under the Anti-Terrorism Act. He was released on bail a few months later, but the case remains ongoing, and he continues to appear in court.

After his court appearance today, Latif Siddique had said, "I was informed this morning that an arrest warrant has been issued against me in the case filed at the International Crimes Tribunal regarding the Hefazat-e-Islam rally at Shapla Chattar. I knew that if I hadn't come to court today, it would be assumed that I had gone into hiding. I usually do not go into hiding. I always make a public appearance. Which is why I came to court today."

Denying his involvement in the Shapla Chattar incident, the former minister said, "I was a minister at the time. But I knew nothing about the Shapla Chattar incident or any matters from that period."

A freedom fighter, Latif Siddique was elected as a Member of Parliament five times representing the Awami League. He was appointed as a minister in 2009.

However, He resigned from the cabinet in 2014 and was expelled from the party following controversial remarks regarding Hajj.

He later became an MP as an independent candidate in the disputed 2024 election. His tenure ended when Parliament was dissolved following the fall of the Awami League government amid the student-led mass uprising that year.

item.title: Police block NCP convoy again upon entering Habiganj
item.description:
Leaders of the National Citizen Party (NCP) were stopped by police once again shortly after entering Habiganj, despite earlier breaking through a police barricade in Sreemangal, Moulvibazar. Police blocked their convoy at around 5:15 pm in Kamaichhara area of Bahubal upazila. As of 6:45 pm, when this report was filed, the leaders remained at the spot.

Witnesses said a bus had been parked across the Dhaka-Sylhet Highway at Kamaichhara, effectively blocking the road. Light rain fell shortly after the blockade began, but NCP leaders stayed on the highway despite the weather. They chanted different slogans. More than 200 members of the police and the Special Security and Protection Battalion (SPBN) were deployed in front of the bus.

Earlier, at around 5:00 pm, police had stopped the NCP convoy on the Dhaka-Sylhet regional highway near the Cha Konnya sculpture in Satgaon, Sreemangal. The convoy included NCP Convener Nahid Islam, Chief Organiser (North) Sarjis Alam, Chief Coordinator Nasir Uddin Patwari, Chief Organiser (South) Hasnat Abdullah, Jatiya Nari Shakti's Member Secretary Mahmuda Mitu, and other central leaders.

NCP leaders alleged that police discouraged them from proceeding toward Habiganj, prompting the convoy to halt near the Cha Konnya sculpture. Speaking in front of the barricade, Sarjis Alam said, "The BNP is in government now, and they are using the administration the way the Awami League did. We did not even go near the area under Section 144, yet they stopped us."

Earlier in the day, the NCP had called a rally in Habiganj municipal town at 3:00 pm. At the same time, the Habiganj district unit of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal announced a counter-programme. To prevent any deterioration in the law and order situation, the district administration imposed Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in designated parts of the town. The NCP later announced it would hold a press conference there instead.

Police did not immediately comment on the incident. However, officials said necessary measures had been taken to maintain law and order.

item.title: Bangladesh PM will decide on visit: Indian High Commissioner
item.description:
Regarding the question of whether Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will visit Delhi in response to India's invitation to attend the BRICS summit or not, Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi said that this decision will be made by the Prime Minister of Bangladesh himself.

However, he noted that they are eagerly waiting for Tarique Rahman’s visit to India and expressed hope that this visit would take place in the near future.

Dinesh Trivedi spoke with journalists after a meeting with Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman and State Minister Shama Obaed Islam at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka on Wednesday afternoon.

This was Dinesh Trivedi's first meeting with the Foreign Minister and State Minister since taking charge as the Indian High Commissioner in Dhaka.

Mentioning that the meeting was held in a very amicable environment, Dinesh Trivedi said various issues of bilateral relations, including sports and even cricket, were discussed.

Referring to the resumption of Indian visas for Bangladeshis, the Indian High Commissioner said, "It is very convenient for the people of both India and Bangladesh. The relationship between the two countries is historical. We share not only a border but also a common culture and dreams. The meeting went very well. I look forward to building the foundation of a relationship that is beneficial for the people of both sides."

Stating that the discussion has only just begun, Dinesh Trivedi said, "We will talk more in the future. I am waiting for that."

As the current Chairman of BIMSTEC, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has invited Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to attend the outreach session of the 18th BRICS Summit to be held in New Delhi on 12-13 September. A final decision has not yet been made regarding whether Bangladesh will attend the summit by accepting that invitation.

A journalist asked whether this matter was discussed in the meeting with the Foreign Minister. In response, the Indian High Commissioner said, "BRICS was not discussed here. I think the Prime Minister of Bangladesh will decide on this matter. From our side, I can say we are eagerly waiting for the Honourable Prime Minister of Bangladesh to visit India. I am very hopeful that it will happen in the near future. We are waiting for that."

item.title: Sale of loose oil must be stopped: Experts
item.description:
Despite laws and regulations banning the sale of loose edible oil, the practice continues unabated in markets, significantly increasing the risk of health problems, including cancer.

Most of this oil is stored in drums originally used for marketing chemicals, which are not food-grade

Furthermore, transparent packaging allows light to penetrate, gradually destroying the micronutrients in the oil. So, the use of light-resistant opaque packaging is essential.

Experts emphasised that the sale of loose oil must be stopped and food regulatory agencies must enhance their monitoring capacity to ensure the use of opaque, food-grade packaging.

These observations were made at a roundtable discussion titled ‘Opaque Food-Grade Packaging for Preserving Vitamin A in Edible Oil and Health Protection.’

The National Heart Foundation of Bangladesh and Prothom Alo organised the event on Tuesday, at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka's Karwan Bazar.

Kazi Emdadul Hoque, Director General of the Bangladesh Standards and Testing Institution (BSTI), said that the concept of food-grade packaging must be presented to the public in an understandable way.

He noted that the entire nation pays the price for Vitamin A deficiency, adding that it is the responsibility of everyone from producers to consumers to keep the quality of edible oil intact.

Sebastin Rema, Director General (additional charge) of the Directorate of National Consumers' Right Protection (DNCRP), remarked that many people wonder why Vitamin A needs to be in oil, which is why they do not object to buying loose oil from the market.

He stressed that there is no alternative to raising public awareness.

Sultan Alam, Joint Secretary (Planning) of the Ministry of Industries, stated that the initiative to fortify edible oil with Vitamin A has been largely successful.

However, he noted that there is room for further work on why this oil does not remain safe by the time it reaches the consumers and why oil is still being sold in the open market.

Professor Khondker Abdul Awal Rizvi, President of the National Heart Foundation of Bangladesh, presided over the roundtable.

He observed that even educated people believe that clear oil in a transparent bottle signifies high quality.

He emphasised the need to increase awareness to change such perceptions and advised reducing oil consumption to prevent various diseases.

Mustak Hassan Md Iftekhar, the founding chairman of the Bangladesh Food Safety Authority and former additional secretary, presented the keynote paper. He explained that transparent packaging cannot block light, leading to destroying Vitamin A and degrading the taste, aroma and quality of the oil.

He further noted that using non-food-grade drums causes monomers, heavy metals, phthalates, solvents, microplastics and carcinogenic compounds to mix with the oil. This results in cancer, hormonal issues and damage to the liver and kidneys, alongside significant economic and social losses.

Professor Mohammad Shoaib, a member of the Bangladesh Food Safety Authority (BFSA), emphasised that proper packaging of edible oil must be ensured. He noted that if Vitamin A is not found in oil, the primary perpetrator must be identified.

Public health expert and former Chief Scientific Officer of IEDCR, Mushtaq Husain highlighted the various health risks, including cancer, caused by the repeated use of the same oil. He advocated for monitoring to ensure that Vitamin A levels in edible oil remain correct and do not pose a risk to anyone.

Professor Sohel Reza Choudhury, head of the Department of Epidemiology and Research at the National Heart Foundation Hospital and Research Institute, urged for changes in dietary habits, including reducing oil consumption, to prevent diseases. He also mentioned the importance of fortifying oil with Vitamin D.

Firoz Alam Suman, Joint Secretary General of the Bangladesh Restaurant Owners Association, said, the real state of the edible oil market could be understood by simply visiting Karwan Bazar.

He noted that one type of oil is being sold as another in open drums. He suggested that instead of fining restaurants, mill owners should be penalised.

Senior General Manager of Meghna Group, Kutubul Alam, said, "We are ready to bottle or package 100 per cent of our oil and have already purchased the machinery. However, this is not possible because there is no demand in the market."

Professor Rokeya Begum of the Food Technology and Nutrition Science Department at Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University cited a survey conducted between 2019 and 2021, stating that awareness among people regarding whether Vitamin A is present in oil is low. She believes opaque packaging of oil is essential.

Md Najmus Sakib, Assistant Professor in the Nutrition and Food Engineering Department at Patuakhali Science and Technology University, said that temperature and light serve as major challenges in maintaining and preserving the quality of edible oil. He suggested that if loose oil is removed from the market, no further problems will remain.

Gulshan Ara, an associate scientist at ICDDR,B, cited a study showing that in more than 60 per cent of cases, packaged edible oil contained the required levels of Vitamin A. She noted that people in both villages and cities still buy loose oil because it is easily accessible.

Dr. Ashek Mahfuz, Portfolio Lead for Large Scale Food Fortification and Value Chain at GAIN, advised increasing public awareness and enhancing the monitoring of relevant government authorities to stop the sale of loose oil in the market.

Other participants in the discussion included former Director General of the Food Planning and Monitoring Unit (FPMU) Shahidur Rahman Faruquee, former President of the Bangladesh Plastic Goods Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BPGMEA) ASM Kamal Uddin, Food Fortification Consultant at TechnoServe Mehedi Hasan, Senior Vice President of BPGMEA KM Iqbal Hossain, Deputy Director (Halal Certification) of BSTI SM Abu Sayed and Organising Secretary of the Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB) Abul Kalam Azad.

The roundtable discussion was moderated by Firoz Choudhury, Assistant Editor at Prothom Alo.

item.title: US-Bangla unveils $1.5b leasing plan for 21 Boeing aircraft
item.description:
US-Bangla Airlines today, Wednesday unveiled a US$1.5 billion fleet expansion plan to add 21 Boeing aircraft under leasing arrangements by the end of 2027, marking one of the largest expansion initiatives by a private Bangladeshi airline.

The plan includes 15 Boeing 737-8 and six Boeing 737-800 aircraft as the airline seeks to significantly expand its international network and transform itself into an integrated global aviation group.

The announcement was made at US-Bangla Airlines’ “Beyond with Boeing” event in the capital.

State Minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism M Rashiduzzaman Millat, PM’s Foreign Affairs and Civil Aviation Adviser Humayun Kabir, US Ambassador to Bangladesh Brent Christensen, Boeing Vice President of Sales Paul Righi, Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) Chairman Air Vice Marshal Md Mostafa Mahmood Siddiq, senior government officials, diplomats and aviation stakeholders attended the event.

Addressing the event, State Minister Millat said the government, under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, is working in a coordinated manner to transform Bangladesh into a regional aviation hub.

“To build a prosperous future for our aviation sector, we are formulating an ‘Aviation Master Plan’ and are going to establish a pilot training academy in Bogura,” he said.

Millat said the country’s aviation capacity would receive another major boost with the opening of the Third Terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA).

“Once the Third Terminal becomes operational, we will be able to handle 24 million passengers annually,” he said.

The state minister termed US-Bangla’s decision to add 21 Boeing aircraft to its fleet an important step towards meeting the country’s growing air travel demand.

“At the same time, Biman Bangladesh Airlines is also set to add 14 new Boeing aircraft to its fleet, which will further accelerate the growth of our aviation sector,” he said.

Millat said the partnership with Boeing also reflected international partners’ growing confidence in Bangladesh’s aviation market.

“Today’s partnership with Boeing reflects the deep confidence and trust that our international partners have in Bangladesh. It will also further strengthen the friendship and economic cooperation between Bangladesh and the United States,” he added.

Boeing Vice President of Sales Paul Righi described US-Bangla’s planned induction of Boeing aircraft as a significant milestone in the airline’s next phase of growth.

“Today marks a significant milestone for US-Bangla Airlines as it embarks on its next phase of growth through the planned induction of modern, fuel-efficient Boeing aircraft,” he said.

Righi said the decision reflected the airline’s confidence in the future of Bangladesh’s aviation industry and its commitment to expanding connectivity while enhancing passengers’ travel experience.

As US-Bangla continues to expand its network across South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Middle East, he said, the Boeing aircraft would support its ambitions through greater fuel efficiency, proven operational reliability and an enhanced passenger experience.

“On behalf of Boeing, I would like to congratulate US-Bangla Airlines on this milestone. We are honoured that Boeing airplanes will be part of your journey, and we appreciate the trust placed both in our company and in our products,” Righi said.

He said Boeing looked forward to building on its relationship with US-Bangla and supporting the airline’s continued growth and success.

US-Bangla Group Managing Director Mohammad Abdullah Al Mamun said the investment represents much more than an expansion of the airline’s fleet.

“This investment represents much more than fleet expansion. It reflects our long-term vision to transform US-Bangla from an airline into a fully integrated global aviation group,” he said.

Mamun said the airline would invest not only in aircraft but also in training, technology, maintenance, cargo, catering and aviation infrastructure to support the sustainable growth of Bangladesh’s aviation sector.

He said Bangladesh’s international air travel market generates an estimated US$5.8 billion annually, but foreign airlines currently carry the majority of international passengers, resulting in a substantial outflow of foreign currency.

The fleet expansion is expected to help increase the market share of Bangladeshi carriers on international routes and strengthen the country’s competitiveness in the global aviation market, he said.

Following induction of the new aircraft, US-Bangla plans to increase frequencies on its existing international routes across South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia and the Middle East.

The carrier also plans to launch flights to Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Colombo, Kathmandu, Kunming, Shenzhen, Beijing, Johor Bahru and Penang as well as destinations in South Korea and Japan.

It is also eyeing Kuwait, Bahrain, Madinah, Dammam and Salalah as part of its Middle East expansion, subject to regulatory and bilateral approvals.

Under its longer-term network strategy, US-Bangla plans to develop Chattogram and Sylhet as regional international hubs, providing greater direct overseas connectivity and reducing dependence on Dhaka.

Beyond passenger operations, the airline plans to establish an aviation training academy, develop aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) facilities, launch a dedicated air cargo airline and build a modern flight catering facility to serve domestic and international carriers.

Mamun said it has already sponsored dozens of Bangladeshi cadet pilots for overseas training and plans to further expand investment in pilot and aircraft engineering education to meet the industry’s growing demand for skilled professionals.

The airline also called for supportive aviation policies, competitive airport charges, improved infrastructure, modern bilateral air service agreements and investment-friendly regulations to unlock Bangladesh’s aviation potential.

“Aviation is not simply a mode of transportation. It is a strategic economic asset that drives tourism, trade, investment, employment, technology and international connectivity,” Mamun said.

He said Bangladesh has the potential to emerge as one of South Asia’s leading aviation markets over the next two decades.

Founded in 2014, US-Bangla Airlines is currently the country’s largest private carrier, operating domestic and international passenger services with a long-term vision of building a globally competitive aviation group encompassing passenger transport, cargo, maintenance, training and aviation support services.

item.title: Japanese population below 120m for first time in decades
item.description:
ASIA-WEATHER/JAPAN

The number of Japanese people living in the country has fallen below 120 million for the first time in 42 years, government data showed Wednesday, as the nation confronts a low birth rate and an ageing society.

As of 1 January, the population of Japanese residents in Japan stood at 119.74 million, down 0.76 per cent from the previous year, according to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications.

The population of Japanese residents has been declining for 17 consecutive years since peaking in 2009, according to the survey, which began in 1968.

However, the population of foreign residents living in Japan reached its highest level since record-keeping began in 2013, according to the ministry.

Including them, the total population stands at 123.8 million.

With a median age of 49.9 years, Japan has the second-oldest population in the world after Monaco, according to the World Bank.

Data in June showed that Japan's fertility rate fell again last year to a new record low, underscoring the demographic crisis gnawing at the world's fourth-largest economy.

The slow-burning emergency is already leading to labour shortages, a ballooning social security bill and a shrinking tax base.

Government figures showed the total fertility rate -- the average number of children a woman is expected to have during her lifetime -- dropped by 0.01 from a year earlier to 1.14, the 10th straight year of decline.

The number of babies born in the country fell by nearly 15,000 to just over 670,000, the lowest figure since records began in 1899.

A chink of light came this month with news that that 265 couples had married thanks to an AI-powered dating app launched by the Tokyo government.

TOKYO Enmusubi went live in September 2024 after a survey found that around 70 per cent of people interested in marriage were not actively engaging in matchmaking.

To overcome this reluctance and ensure that only people interested in tying the knot joined, those signing up had to prove that they were legally single and pass an online interview, among other conditions.

As of 30 June this year, the app had 16,000 registered members -- whittled down from around 36,000 applicants -- and 760 couples in "serious relationships", according to government data released this month.

The government quoted one woman with the pseudonym "Turtle" as saying she tried the app "as a last chance" as she approached her 40th birthday.

"After going on several blind dates, I met my current husband at the end of August, and we started a serious relationship in mid-September," she said.

"I accepted his proposal at the end of December."

NCP leaders, police scuffle as convoy stopped in Sreemangal
item.description:
Saiful Islam
Police stopped the convoy of National Citizen Party (NCP) leaders in Sreemangal on Wednesday afternoon as they were heading to Habiganj to join a previously announced protest program, triggering a brief scuffle over police barricades.
The confrontation took place around 4:30pm near the Tea Maiden (Cha Kanya) sculpture on the Sreemangal-Shayestaganj road after police blocked the route with trucks and barricades.
NCP Convener Nahid Islam, Chief Organizer (Northern Region) Sarjis Alam, Chief Organizer (Southern Region) and MP Hasnat Abdullah, Chief Coordinator Nasiruddin Patwary and MP Dr Mahmuda Mitu got out of their vehicles and held talks with police officials at the scene.
At one stage, pushing and shoving broke out between police personnel and NCP leaders and activists. Hasnat Abdullah and Nasiruddin Patwary were seen in a scuffle with police as officers attempted to move them away from the barricade.
During an exchange with police, Hasnat questioned the legality of the blockade.
“If you can, provide us with security. If not, we will proceed at our own responsibility. Under what law are you stopping us?” he said.
Police officials cited security concerns, but Hasnat replied: “Who are the security threats? Instead of arresting them, you are blocking our road. You imposed Section 144 in Habiganj and are stopping us in Sreemangal. This is illegal.”
A police officer at the scene told the NCP leaders that “a major incident” could occur if they crossed the barricade.
The NCP convoy later crossed the barricade and resumed its journey to Habiganj.
According to party sources, Nahid, Opposition Chief Whip in parliament; Member Secretary Akhtar Hossain; Sarjis; Hasnat; Nasiruddin; Dr Mahmuda Mitu and other leaders left the Moulvibazar Circuit House for Habiganj around 3pm.
Police later set up barricades using trucks near the Tea Maiden sculpture, halting the convoy and causing traffic congestion, with hundreds of vehicles stranded on both sides of the road.
Moulvibazar Assistant Superintendent of Police (Sreemangal Circle) Md Wahiduzzaman Raju said the leaders had been stopped for security reasons.
The latest incident came a day after NCP leaders alleged that activists of the BNP, Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal and Jubo Dal attacked their convoy in Habiganj town following Tuesday’s program, leaving several people injured.
Amid heightened tensions between the BNP and the NCP, the administration-imposed Section 144 in the Habiganj municipal area from Wednesday morning.
Local sources said Chhatra Dal activists allegedly attacked vehicles carrying NCP leaders near Habiganj Town Hall on Tuesday evening. Several vehicles belonging to journalists were also vandalized.
Sarjis Alam and Nasiruddin Patwary reportedly took shelter in a branch of Sonali Bank during the attack before police escorted them to safety.
The NCP later suspended two previously announced “July March” programs in Moulvibazar and instead announced a protest rally in Habiganj, while separate programs by BNP and Chhatra Dal further heightened tensions in the district.

item.title: Trivedi: PM Tarique's India visit key to positive progress
item.description:
Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi on Wednesday expressed optimism about the future of bilateral ties, saying Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's proposed visit to India would pave the way for progress on outstanding issues, including the renewal of the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty.
Speaking to reporters after separate courtesy meetings with Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman and State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Trivedi said discussions covered a range of issues and were held in a positive atmosphere.
"Once Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to India is confirmed and the joint working group sits down with the necessary documents, everything will move in a positive direction," he said.
The envoy said there was no bilateral issue that could not be resolved through dialogue in a way that served the mutual interests of both countries.
"There is no problem that cannot be resolved if it benefits both countries," he said.
On the renewal of the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, Trivedi said the joint working group of the two countries was already discussing the matter.
"I hope they will meet soon. There is no issue that cannot be resolved. Whatever is necessary in the interests of the people of both countries will be done," he said.
Describing the meetings as constructive, the Indian high commissioner said the discussions focused on issues important to the people of both countries.
"At the end of the day, this is about the people of the two countries. Whatever is necessary for the democracies of both countries, those interests will be taken into consideration," he added.

item.title: Law minister: Govt taken effective initiatives to reduce civil case backlog
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Wednesday said the present government has taken effective initiatives to reduce longstanding civil case backlog.
"Various reform initiatives are being implemented to make the judicial process faster, more efficient and more people-friendly. Backlog of cases could be reduced and the efficiency of the judicial process enhanced through the exchange of domestic and international experiences and mutual cooperation," he said.
The minister made the remarks at a seminar titled "Addressing Delays in the Disposal of Civil Cases: Shared Experiences of Bangladesh and Japan" at Judicial Administration Training Institute (JATI). Law and Justice Division and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) jointly organized the seminar, an official release said on Wednesday.
Md Asaduzzaman said that many civil cases in Bangladesh are still pending despite having remained unresolved for many years. The prolonged pendency of these cases has increased the sufferings of litigants and placed an additional burden on the judicial system, he added.
"To address this situation, the government is implementing various reform initiatives, including modernizing the judiciary, expanding Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR), introducing technology-driven judicial services, and making the judicial process simpler and more efficient," he further said.
The law minister also said the experiences and cooperation of the Japanese Ministry of Justice and international partners, including the JICA, would play a significant role in strengthening Bangladesh's judicial system.
"Such joint initiatives would create new opportunities for the exchange of knowledge and experiences between the two countries, which would make a positive contribution to enhancing the efficiency of the judicial process," he added.
Speaking as the special guest, Deputy Director-General of the International Cooperation Department of Japan's Ministry of Justice, Kazunori Nose, assured that Japan would continue its cooperation in strengthening and enhancing the capacity of Bangladesh's judicial system.
The keynote papers were presented by Senior Assistant Secretary of the Law and Justice Division Syed Md Shafayet and Professor Wakazono Rei of Japan's Ministry of Justice. Project Director of the relevant project and Additional Secretary of the Law and Justice Division Md Khadem Ul Kayes chaired the seminar.

item.title: Health officials report 534 fresh cases of dengue inflection, 3 deaths overnight
item.description:
Health officials on Wednesday said they recorded 534 fresh cases of dengue onslaughts killing at least three persons in the past 24 hours.
"During the period, (of the 534) 68 patients were hospitalized in Barisal division, 71 in Chittagong division, 131 in Dhaka division, 56 in Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) and 65 in Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) areas, 45 in Khulna division, 37 in Mymensingh division, 30 in Rajshahi division, 26 in Rangpur division and five in Sylhet division, a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) statement said.
Since the start of the dengue onslaughts, Bangladesh this year has witnessed so far 50 deaths while the disease inflicted 14,690.
Last year, dengue claimed 413 lives and inflicted 1,02,861 people in the country.
Besides, dengue claimed 575 lives and inflicted 1,01,214 people in 2024.

item.title: PM meets Tahsin, who lost sister in Milestone tragedy
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday met Tahsin Abdullah, a schoolboy whose heartwarming smile at the closing ceremony of the Notun Kuri Sports 2025-26 touched millions, a year after the boy lost his elder sister in the Milestone School fighter jet crash.
Learning the heartbreaking story behind the widely shared photograph of the smiling boy on social media, the prime minister met Tahsin and his father Nazmul Haque at the prime minister's office at Bangladesh Secretariat on Wednesday, said PM’s Assistant Press Secretary Gazi Shahriar Pamir.
A photograph of Tahsin during the closing ceremony of the “Notun Kuri Sports 2025-26” at Bangladesh Army Stadium in the capital on July 27 went viral on social media, showing Tahsin in his school uniform stretching out both hands towards the prime minister with an expression of pure joy. But behind that heartwarming smile was a story of deep personal grief.
In July 2025, Tahsin lost his elder sister Tasnia in the tragic fighter jet crash at Milestone School in Uttara. Although both siblings studied at the same school, they were in separate buildings on that fateful day. Tahsin was then a sixth-grade student, while Tasnia was an eighth-grader. The fighter jet crashed into the building where Tasnia was attending classes.
Hearing the deafening explosion, young Tahsin rushed to find his elder sister. After hearing that saline and water were needed, he stood waiting with bottles of saline and water in his small hands for his sister. But that wait never ended.
According to his family, the tragedy changed Tahsin completely. During a healing session after the incident, he wrote: “I am in great pain. I have lost my beloved sister. She died. I miss her so, so much. She was my best friend.”
Since losing his sister, Tahsin's once cheerful and lively smile was rarely seen. But on July 27 was a different day. At the Bangladesh Army Stadium, as Prime Minister Tarique Rahman was moving around the field during the closing ceremony, Tahsin became overwhelmed with joy when the prime minister came near him.
His innocent smile and excitement were captured on camera, and the photograph later spread widely on social media, with many people connecting emotionally with the boy’s happiness.
Later, the prime minister came to know that behind the smiling face in the photograph was a heartbreaking family history. After learning the details, he directed his Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon to take steps to inquire about Tahsin and his family.
As Tahsin arrived at prime minister’s office, the prime minister enquired about Tahsin's studies and ambitions. Tahsin said he wanted to become a successful businessman and do something that would benefit people and attract them.
The prime minister appreciated his dream and advised the young boy to concentrate on his studies, play sports regularly and work with sincerity and dedication to achieve his goals, Pamir said.
During the conversation, Tahsin said football was his favorite sports. The prime minister gifted him a basketball bearing his autograph and a drone set.
After the meeting, an excited Tahsin said he was very happy to meet the prime minister again. He said he never imagined he would get such an opportunity and described the entire experience as a complete surprise. He said he was eagerly waiting to go to school and share the story of meeting the prime minister with his friends.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman also expressed deep sympathy and condolence to Tahsin’s father over the tragic loss of his daughter in the Milestone fighter jet crash.
PM’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon, Private Secretary-2 Md Mehedul Islam, Assistant Private Secretary-2 Abdur Rahman Sani, Associate Professor (Orthopedics) Dr Shah Muhammad Aman Ullah, Deputy Press Secretary Jahidul Islam Rony and Amra BNP Poribar Member Secretary Moksedul Momin Mithun were present.

India lower house passes bill raising penalties for exam leaks
item.description:
India’s lower house of parliament approved a bill on Wednesday that would toughen penalties for leaking exam papers, after youth-led protests calling for sweeping reforms forced the education minister to resign.
The legislation would double the maximum jail term for those involved in leaking exam papers to 10 years, and raises the maximum fine to more than $1 million.
Lawmakers approved the bill by a voice vote after a raucous, hours-long debate, according to India’s public broadcaster.
It will next be put to a vote in the upper house, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling alliance holds a majority. Modi’s cabinet greenlighted the stricter punishments last week.
The approval follows weeks of mass protests over leaked exam papers and other irregularities, which culminated in the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan on Saturday.
The protests, spearheaded by the online Cockroach Janta Party movement, drew massive support from students across the country and presented a major challenge to Modi’s government.
Rahul Gandhi of the main opposition Congress Party said he could relate to the frustration among India’s youth over the country’s education system.
“This was not anger... this was not hatred, this was deep expression of the youth of this country, of the future generation of this country, and I feel that all political parties must respect this expression,” he said in a speech in the house.
Despite rapid economic growth in the world’s most populous country, millions of young people face a shortage of well-paid jobs and fierce competition for careers.
The intense pressure to succeed has fueled a vast network of coaching centers and created opportunities for criminal groups to profit by selling leaked exam questions.
Despite repeated government crackdowns, such leaks have remained a recurring problem in both national and state-level examinations.
Demonstrations against the paper leaks in New Delhi turned violent on July 20 when huge crowds attempted to march towards parliament from the Jantar Mantar protest site.
Police fired tear gas and used batons to disperse the protest, triggering clashes and a wave of detentions.

item.title: France expands mass evacuations as Spain battles wildfires
item.description:
As Spain battled its largest wildfire on record and France carried out one of Europe’s biggest evacuations since World War II, scientists warned that extreme wildfires are becoming more frequent worldwide.
On Tuesday, French authorities evacuated another 4,000 people from Atlantic coast resorts adding to the 220,000 other people fleeing a blazing wildfire in southwest France.
Fresh fires broke out near the Atlantic resort of Grand Crohot west of Bordeaux, prompting authorities to deploy 23 planes and helicopters to contain the flames.
“The situation remains complicated. We’re not out of the woods,” said Sophie Brocas, the top government official in the coastal region of Gironde, where Grand Crohot and Bordeaux are located.
The Gironde wildfire has burned an area four times the size of Paris, and resisted the firefighting efforts of a dozen countries.
In Spain, there was a respite for the evacuees as thousands of residents were allowed to return home after firefighters managed to contain major blazes.
However, authorities remained on alert for a fourth summer heatwave with temperatures expected to exceed 40 degrees Celsius on Wednesday.
The biggest concern for firefighters in Spain was two large fires that had at times come close to merging into a single blaze in wooded hills to the west of Madrid.
In Avila, to the northwest of Madrid, a pyrocumulonimbus cloud was seen over the blaze. Scientists describe these clouds as fire-generated thunderstorms forming over intense heat sources like wildfires or volcanic eruptions.
“We are feeling a lot of anger and helplessness. It’s something inhuman,” 48-year-old gardener David Gonzalez said about the destruction caused by the fires in Avila.
Experts fear that incoming heat waves might cause the blazing fires to worsen.

Russian fencer wins world championship gold under his country flag
item.description:
A Russian has won a gold medal at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, the first since the country was allowed to compete again under its own flag in the combat sport.
Pavel Graudyn, 19, defeated South Korean Do Gyeong-dong 15-7 in the men's individual sabre final on Tuesday, having earlier stunned France's top-seed Sebastien Patrice in the last 16.
It was the first major championship since the International Fencing Federation (FIE) lifted all restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes on June 2.
The sanctions had been imposed in 2022 after the invasion of Ukraine and consequent war, with Russian and Belarusian fencers allowed to participate only as neutrals.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) earlier this month lifted some restrictions allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in team events and qualifying for the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.
Ukraine slammed the IOC decision as "premature" and "unfounded" after more than four years of conflict since Russia's invasion.
Governing bodies for swimming, gymnastics, judo, taekwondo and wrestling have also recently lifted restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes.

Apparel leaders want to source gas from CNG stations amid severe shortage
item.description:
Amid a severe gas shortage triggered by the shutdown of a Floating Storage Regasification Unit (FSRU) terminal in Maheshkhali, the country's two leading apparel trade bodies—the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA)—have urged the government to allow export-oriented garment factories to source Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) in cylinders from filling stations.
In separate letters issued on July 28, the trade associations informed the government that granting factories temporary access to CNG stations until regular gas supplies normalize would help maintain production and export operations.
The appeal follows an order issued on July 27 by Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company, which directed all CNG filling stations to immediately stop selling natural gas in open cylinders or gas cascades to non-authorized vehicles.
Titas stated that such supplies pose severe safety risks and violate the Gas Act 2010 and the Gas Distribution Rules 2026.
Titas warned in its letter that supplying gas in unauthorized cylinders is illegal and highly dangerous, adding that non-compliance could lead to connection disconnections and legal action.
In a letter sent to the President of the Bangladesh CNG Filling Station and Conversion Workshop Owners Association, BGMEA president Mahmud Hasan Khan stated that the readymade garment sector is the primary engine of the national economy, driving maximum export earnings, generating millions of jobs, and earning foreign exchange.
He noted that the shutdown of one of the two FSRU LNG terminals in Maheshkhali has caused a severe gas crisis across industrial hubs. Gas pressure in many factories has dropped to zero PSI, making it increasingly difficult to sustain production and deliver shipments to international buyers on schedule.
The BGMEA requested that factories with urgent operational needs be granted temporary permission to collect gas in cylinders from CNG filling stations to safeguard production and honor export commitments.
The association added that Titas's recent order has made many filling stations reluctant to supply gas in cylinders.
BKMEA seeks ministry intervention
Meanwhile, in a notice to its members, the BKMEA stated that following Titas's directive, the association's president discussed the matter with the Secretary of the Energy and Mineral Resources Division.
According to BKMEA, after explaining that disruptions to gas supply in export-oriented industries would severely harm production and exports, the Energy Secretary instructed Titas's managing director to take necessary measures so that export-oriented factories can continue sourcing gas from CNG filling stations as before.
The trade body advised member factories to strictly adhere to government regulations and safety guidelines while collecting gas, and urged those with alternative LMG (mobile gas) setups to utilize them at full capacity.
The BKMEA noted that the current gas shortage may persist until August 8, after which conditions are expected to gradually normalize. It added that it remains in regular contact with relevant authorities to monitor the situation.
